sentences: The writer, a successful crime fiction author, lives in a country manor house filled with elaborate games and automata.
He invites his wife's lover, the owner of two hair salons, to his home and says he would like the lover to take his wife off his hands so he can be with his more desirable mistress.

To provide the lover, whose salons are not yet fully profitable, the means to support the high-maintenance wife, the writer suggests that the lover steal valuable jewellery from the house, with the writer recouping his losses through an insurance claim.
The lover agrees, and the writer leads him through an elaborate scheme to fake a robbery.
At the conclusion, the writer pulls a gun on the lover and reveals that the bogus theft was merely a ruse to frame the lover as a burglar so he can kill him.

Berating the lover's profession as a hairdresser and background as the "un-English" son of an Italian immigrant (originally with an Italian surname) who went to a "second-rate public school," the writer cannot accept that his wife left him for such an "unworthy" rival.
He puts the gun to the lover's head; there is a gunshot, and the screen cuts to black.
A few days later, an inspector arrives to investigate the lover's disappearance.
The writer purports to know nothing, but as the inspector collates incriminating clues, the writer breaks down and explains the burglary hoax.
He insists that he only pretended to shoot the lover using a blank cartridge and that his rival left humiliated but unharmed.
After finding evidence supporting a murder, the inspector arrests the writer.
As the writer is about to be taken to the station, the inspector reveals himself as the heavily disguised lover, seeking revenge on the writer.

The score is seemingly evened, though the writer is unable to admit being duped and pretends he saw through the lover's disguise while expressing admiration for the lover having been a worthy opponent and games player.
The still dissatisfied lover expresses that the writer has not experienced the level of humiliation of his own imminent death.
He announces they will play another game involving a real murder.
The lover says he fatally strangled the writer's mistress and has planted incriminating evidence throughout the writer's house.
The police, who have been tipped off, will arrive soon.
The writer dismisses his claim, but phones the mistress, only to learn from her flatmate that the mistress is dead.
Following the lover's cryptic clues, the writer frantically searches the house for the planted evidence.
The writer finds the last item just as the lover says the police are arriving.
The dishevelled writer pleads with the lover to stall them while he composes himself.
The lover is heard ostensibly talking to the officers, but there are actually no police.

The lover then reveals that he faked the mistress's death, with the flatmate and the mistress's willing assistance as payback for the games of humiliation the writer has inflicted on the mistress, thus tricking the writer a second time.
The writer is further humiliated when the lover reveals that the mistress informed him that the writer is practically impotent and has not had relations with her in over a year.
As the lover prepares to leave, fetching the wife's fur coat and belongings, he continues humiliating the writer with information provided by the writer's wife and mistress.
Inspired again by the burglary scenario, the writer threatens to shoot the lover to stop him from bragging about his humiliation to anyone else―especially the wife.

However, the lover says he really did report the writer's burglary setup and assault to the police, who were initially sceptical but assured him they would follow-up; for this reason, the lover points out, the police now would not believe the writer's concocted story of killing a burglar.
Nevertheless, the writer, pushed too far when the lover ridicules his literary detective, shoots and mortally wounds the lover.
The police arrive outside, and the distraught and defeated writer locks himself inside the house.

As the lover lies dying, he tells the writer to tell the police that "it was just a bloody game"; he then presses the automata control box, leaving the writer surrounded by a cacophony of his activated electronic toys as police pound on the door for entry.

In the city, during a raging thunderstorm one night, a woman frantically tells her husband that from the living-room window she has seen a man with his throat slit in a chair by the window in the deserted house across the way.
The husband calls the police, but a search of the old house finds no evidence of a murder.
The next morning, the woman notices a freshly planted bed of Laburnum in the garden next to the old house that was not there before.
She calls the investigating detective, an inspector, and suggests that the body of the murder victim she witnessed may be buried there.
The inspector questions the neighbour, who confirms that he planted the trees the night before during the storm, but refuses to let the police search the garden or dig up the trees.

The woman is recovering from a nervous breakdown that occurred after her unfaithful first husband was killed a few years earlier in a car accident with his young paramour, and continues to suffer from recurring nightmares of the event.
After learning that the woman has called the inspector multiple times about the investigation, the husband suggests that she see his psychiatrist friend.
Indignant, the woman continues to insist that she saw a murder in the house, but since there is no proof, the husband remains sceptical.
The woman's visiting friend is equally sceptical, suggesting that the woman sees what she thinks she sees because of her recent breakdown.

That night, when both the woman and the friend see a light moving behind the old house's shutters, they call the police, who discover the neighbour wandering around with a flashlight and arrest him for trespassing.
A second search of the house and excavation of the garden reveal nothing, and the inspector privately tells the husband that the case is officially closed.
That evening, the woman tells the husband and the friend that she saw another body in the old house, that of a woman.
The woman is then sedated by the husband and the friend, who believe that the woman is losing her mind.
The next day, the woman agrees to see the psychiatrist and recounts to him her first husband's fatal car accident.
The psychiatrist advises her to check into a clinic in a foreign country for a few weeks, to which the woman agrees.
Shortly afterwards, the woman calls the inspector and urges him to search the old house again.
After falsely promising to do so, he reveals that the premise was purchased six months earlier by a private company.

The following evening, as the woman prepares to depart for the foreign country, the husband asks her to sign several financial documents, including a power of attorney granting him control over their financial holdings.
She complies, before noticing in the documents that the husband had recently acquired the private company.
The woman angrily accuses the husband and the friend of having an affair, revealing that she had discovered their tickets for an island.
She assails them for plotting to torment her in order to have her committed, and claims the friend was trying to poison her.
When the husband denies the woman's accusations, she runs to the old house and lets herself inside; the husband and the friend both chase after her.
The woman lures the two to the second-floor room where she claimed to have seen the bodies.
There, she slashes the husband's throat and stabs the friend to death, before positioning them in exactly the same manner that she claimed to have seen the two bodies.
She then calls the police and once again claims to have seen two murdered bodies in the abandoned house, wearying them into apathy over investigating her actual killings.
The neighbour, who had grown up in the husband and the woman's house as a child, makes a surprise visit, congratulating the woman on pulling off her scheme.
He assures her that he does not intend to report the murders, as the inspector would not believe him.
The woman asks the neighbour to look after her house and the garden while she is away, indefinitely.
The neighbour happily agrees to the bargain as the woman bids him goodbye and departs.
During the 1930s, three privileged old university friends gather for the week-end in an old country house located in a sprawling British estate.
In fact the host, who has recently inherited the estate, invites his two college acquaintances the first guest and the second guest ostensibly for a week-end of game hunting.

The second guest, who appears to have an interest in the supernatural from a more scientific perspective, is sullen and rude, though an excellent shot, while the first guest is easygoing but puzzled as to why he was asked along, especially when his colleagues continually mock and ridicule him.
As soon as they arrive, personalities clash, petty arguments ensue and the gloomy environment starts to wear on everyone's nerves.
To make matters worse, the host neglects to mention that the place might be haunted.
During the night, the first guest begins to have strange hallucinations involving a creepy porcelain doll and the former occupants of the mansion.
The first guest finds himself transported back in time, bearing witness to the trials and tribulations of a young woman who once resided in the house.
As the story progresses, the tenuous ties that bind the men together begin to unravel and the strange visions begin to become more vivid until they threaten to drive the first guest mad.
It turns out to be haunted by the previous occupants, though only the first guest can see them.

Finally, the host admits that he invited the first guest and the second guest because he had heard rumours that the house was haunted and he chose them both as likely subjects to draw any spirits out in the open.

As the visions become more frequent and detailed, the first guest is thrust into a strange supernatural realm of incest, arson and madness from which escape is impossible: the doll claims the lives of the first guest and the host while the second guest, who leaves the estate early in a taxi, seems to be driven not to the train station but into the past to become an inmate of the nearby insane asylum which was destroyed by fire years before.
In 1930, a toddler, daughter of a British army colonel and his American wife, is kidnapped and murdered.
In December 1935, the detective travels from one city to another on a luxury express train.
His old friend, a director of the company that owns the rail line, arranges the detective's accommodation after all the first-class compartments are unusually sold out during the off-season.

Other passengers include an American socialite; an English governess; a Swedish missionary; an American businessman, with his secretary/translator and English valet; an Italian-American car salesman; an elderly Russian princess and her German maid; a Hungarian count and his wife; a British army colonel; and an American theatrical agent.
The day after the train's departure, the businessman requests to hire the detective as a bodyguard as he has received death threats, but the detective declines despite a very generous fee.
When the train stops in a city on the route, the director gives the detective his compartment and shares a coach with a Greek physician.
During the night, a snowdrift in a country on the route strands the train, while the detective is awakened by a moan from the businessman's compartment.
The conductor is told through the door that it was just a nightmare.
The businessman is dead the next morning; drugged and stabbed twelve times.
The detective finds a charred letter fragment revealing the businessman's true identity: an American gangster, who along with an accomplice, had carried out the toddler's kidnapping and murder.
The gangster had betrayed his accomplice and fled the country with the ransom money.
The toddler's mother then died giving premature birth to a stillborn baby, and the toddler's father committed suicide.
A French maidservant, suspected of complicity in the kidnapping, also committed suicide before being found innocent.
The director feels that there is justice in the gangster's death.
The detective finds the gangster's broken watch showing 1:15, and concludes that the gangster was murdered at that time when the moaning was heard.
The socialite says that she found a sleeping-car conductor's button in her compartment and a bloodied knife in her makeup bag.
The car salesman says that he knew the gangster was "a mobster", and theorizes that he was killed in a gangland feud.

Interviewing the conductor and the passengers individually, the detective learns the secretary is the son of the District Attorney from the kidnapping case and knew the toddler's mother; the valet was a British army batman; the missionary has been to the country of the kidnapping; the countess's maiden name is a German surname (German for an English surname, the toddler's mother's maiden name); the conductor's daughter died five years earlier of scarlet fever; the colonel and the governess will marry once he has divorced his philandering wife; and the princess was the toddler's mother's godmother.
He also learns that the toddler's family household had a butler, a secretary, a cook, a chauffeur, and a nursemaid.
The detective tricks the German maid into revealing she had been a cook.
The car salesman denies having been a chauffeur, while the theatrical agent claims to actually be the gangster's bodyguard.

The detective assembles the suspects and describes two solutions to the murder: the first that the gangster's murder was a gangland revenge killing - someone disguised as a sleeping-car conductor entered the train at the city on the route and later stabbed the gangster, discarded the dagger in the socialite's makeup bag, then escaped when the train was stopped by the snowdrift.
The director and the physician reject this scenario as absurd, but the detective says they might reconsider that opinion.
The second solution links together all the suspects.

In addition to the incriminating revelations the detective extracted from the theatrical agent, the secretary, the German maid, and the princess, the detective deduces that: the countess is the toddler's mother's younger sister, the governess was the toddler's family's secretary the valet was the toddler's family's butler the missionary was the toddler's nursemaid the colonel was the toddler's father's close friend the car salesman was the toddler's family's chauffeur the conductor was the French maidservant's father the theatrical agent was not the gangster's bodyguard, as the businessman had tried to hire the detective for that job.
He was actually a former policeman who had fallen in love with the French maidservant.
The socialite is revealed to be a woman of another name, mother of the toddler's mother and the countess, and the organizer of this "extraordinary revenge".
The secretary drugged the gangster, allowing the conspirators to execute him jointly, each with a stab to the chest totalling 12, the count and the countess stabbing the gangster together.
They killed the gangster at 2:00 am while the detective was asleep.
The moan and broken watch were to convince the detective that the murder occurred at a time when the suspects had alibis.
The detective asks the director to choose one solution before the train is freed from the snowdrift, saying the Yugoslav police would probably prefer the simpler first solution of the gangland feud.
The director chooses the first scenario.
The physician and the detective concur, although the detective struggles with his conscience.
The snowdrift is cleared and the train resumes its journey.
In a Cold War city, a young American woman is rushed to the emergency room after apparently overdosing in a suicide attempt.
With her is an American psychoanalyst who lives in the city working as a university teacher.
While doctors and nurses fight to save the young woman's life, an investigator begins investigating the incident.
Through fragmented flashbacks, the narrative depicts the story of the psychoanalyst and the young woman's romance.
After meeting her at a party, the psychoanalyst is enchanted by the young woman, a sophisticated but free-spirited military brat.

The two begin a whirlwind affair, but shortly into the relationship, the young woman is revealed to suffer from severe depression and be married to a much older man, whom she occasionally visits across the border in a nearby city.
Though the psychoanalyst initially enjoys the young woman's free-spirited lifestyle, he soon becomes embittered by it, as it includes impulsive promiscuity and heavy drinking.
The psychoanalyst begins stalking the young woman, and eventually confronts her about her marriage to her husband.
She insists that the marriage is simply platonic, and that she and her husband are no longer in love.
Despite this, the psychoanalyst begins researching into her husband's past, and inquires with local government agencies about how the young woman can proceed with a divorce, which she refuses.
The psychoanalyst's jealousy of the young woman only continues to grow, and he begins to resent her.
After one argument, the young woman forcefully impels the psychoanalyst to have sex with her to sate him, and is disgusted with herself after.
In one incident, when the couple vacation in a North African country, their vehicle breaks down, and they hitch a ride from two Moroccan men.
The psychoanalyst is left in the bed of the truck, while the young woman sits between the two men, flirting with them during the drive, which the psychoanalyst keenly observes.

Upon arriving in a desert town, the psychoanalyst suggests that he and the young woman return to their home country where he can take a teaching position in a big city, but she insists that they live "in the moment."
The young woman begins to question her and the psychoanalyst's romance when she finds evidence that he has been treating her as a case study.
Later, the psychoanalyst confronts her about a photograph in her apartment that he has obsessed over, which shows her at a lake with another man.
She tells him the photo is of her and her late brother, taken in an American state years prior, but the psychoanalyst does not believe her.
The following morning, the psychoanalyst confronts the drunken young woman outside her apartment, telling her he cannot bear the thought of her with another man.
When she defiantly renounces him, he slaps her.
Later, the young woman invites him back to her apartment, only to taunt him in kabuki makeup, mockingly presenting herself as the "new her."
When he storms out, the young woman screams at him from her balcony, hurling objects at him onto the street below.
The following night, the young woman leaves the psychoanalyst a drunken voice message suggesting she wants to die.

In the present, as doctors attempt to revive the dying young woman, the investigator pieces together the chain of events, culminating in an interview with the psychoanalyst, who presents himself simply as the young woman's friend.

Uncovering timeline inconsistencies in the psychoanalyst's story, the investigator determines what actually occurred: the psychoanalyst, after finding the young woman overdosing on poison in her apartment, looked on as she slowly collapsed, and subsequently raped her once she lost consciousness.
Though the investigator has physical evidence suggesting the young woman was raped, he is unable to elicit a confession from the psychoanalyst.
Her husband arrives, and reveals the young woman has survived the overdose following a life-saving tracheotomy.
The psychoanalyst departs without repercussion, but, before he leaves, her husband comments that he must love the young woman more than his own dignity.
Some time later, in the big city, the psychoanalyst sees the young woman passing by in front of a luxury hotel as he enters a taxi.
He calls out to her, and she briefly turns toward him, revealing her tracheotomy scar, before impassively walking away.
A female hiker finds a dead woman on a moor in the countryside.
The strangled victim is identified as a certain woman.
Four months later, an insurance company asks the detective to examine an expensive diamond belonging to a millionaire.

The detective identifies it as a fake, but is assured by the millionaire that the original was purchased at a famous jeweller's in a big city for his mistress, an actress; she apparently returned a paste replica after their split.
The detective agrees to meet the actress at an exclusive hotel on an island in the sea to probe the mystery.
The hotel was a king's summer palace, gifted to his former mistress, the ex-actress hotel owner.
The actress is on holiday with her new husband.
She is emotionally abusive to her stepdaughter and flirts openly with a married man, who is holidaying on the island with his wife.
The actress's husband turns to his old friend, the hotel owner for support.
She is horrified by how the actress treats the actress's husband and the stepdaughter and reveals that the actress arranged for the married man to be on the island.
Also at the resort are theatrical producers, a husband and wife, who are experiencing financial hardship because the actress left a major show of theirs and is refusing a role in another.
Likewise, the actress is causing trouble for a writer, who has already spent his advance royalties for the actress's tell-all biography, which she now refuses to approve for release.
Early on the third morning, the actress goes by paddle-boat to a bay for an assignation with the married man.
He arrives by powerboat with the female producer, and, upon approaching the actress, calls out to the female producer that the actress has been strangled.
The detective begins to investigate the murder, but all of the guests have an alibi.
The actress's husband claims to have been in his room typing at the time of the crime.
The married man's wife was with the stepdaughter at a cove, and did not leave until 11:55 for a 12:30 tennis match.

The millionaire argued with the actress at the bay and returned the fake diamond at 11:30, with the actress promising an explanation that evening; his alibi is confirmed by both his yacht crew and the hotel owner.
The detective found the bauble in a grotto when examining the crime scene.
The married man left the hotel with the female producer minutes before 12:00 PM, seeing the millionaire's yacht approaching, and hearing the commemorative noon cannon firing.
The writer met the swimming stepdaughter when entering the cove at noon, and reports that a bottle flung from the top of a cliff nearly hit him.
The male producer was seen reading by the hotel owner and her staff.
He claims low water pressure hindered his 12:15 wash before tennis, but nobody admits to bathing at that time.
Assembling the suspects together, the detective accuses the married couple of the crime.

He asserts that the married man's wife knocked out the actress and hid her in the grotto (where he had detected the actress's perfume in the air), then donned her outfit and applied makeup to simulate a suntan and posed as the actress's body for the female producer to see.
After the female producer went for help, the married man strangled the actress and placed her body on the beach.

The detective calls the married man's wife's alibi into question by proposing that she set the stepdaughter's watch twenty minutes ahead, suggested the girl wear a swim cap to muffle the sound of the noon cannon, and corrected the watch before leaving to attack the actress.

Once the female producer left the beach, the married man's wife still would have had time to toss away the lotion bottle—which almost hit the writer—and wash off her "tan"—accounting for the drop in water pressure—before the tennis match.
The married couple scoff at the detective's accusations, and taunt that he has provided neither motive, nor proof.

The married man pays for his hotel stay by cheque, signing the first letter of his surname in a distinctive way that the detective recognises as being the same way another man, husband of the well-insured moor victim, signed his name.
The detective states that sending for pictures will prove this, as well as that the hiker who found the body, at a time when the husband had an alibi, was the married man's wife.
Exposed, the married man does not resist when the detective removes a pipe, which he never actually smokes, from his lips, empties its bowl, and reveals the real diamond.
The married man then punches the detective before he and the married man's wife are arrested and taken away from the island by boat.
The hotel owner informs the detective that he will be rewarded by the kingdom for his work before he and the others depart the island.

The man (an actor) is a successful advertising executive and the woman (an actress) is his young and hedonistic wife, but their lives are thrown into turmoil when the man inherits his great-great grandfather's secret diaries.
He becomes obsessed with research into solid geometry contained in the diaries and is fascinated by the theory of "a plane without a surface."
His pursuit of this mythical geometric concept tears his marriage apart.
The film is interspersed with flashbacks showing the man's great-great grandfather discovering the same mysteries of the supernatural side of geometry as the man is uncovering by reading the diaries.

Eventually the man follows the instructions buried in the diaries and begins carefully folding a large sheet of paper in on itself like a lotus flower, then the folded paper emits a bright light, folds over itself and disappears.
On seeing this, he dedicates his life to understanding more about the diaries and his great-great grandfather's mysterious disappearance.
He goes on to become obsessed with this transformation and the discussion in the book which links it to 'sexual intercourse positions' of which the diary claims there are only 17.
After a love-making session with his wife, he proceeds to place another of the paper lotus flowers in the center of her curled body.
As she curls into a foetal position unknowingly around the paper flower, she somehow completes the flower folding as had previously been achieved with just the paper.
She spins around the paper flower several times and disappears, emitting tones of shock and fear.
The film ends with the man alone in bed.
In 1380, in the kingdom, the priest (an actor) flees his village when found in flagrante delicto with a married woman.
During the flight, he witnesses a group euthanise a member to give him relief from his long-recurring internal pain.
He becomes known to the group and is captured.
The group is a traveling acting troupe who thinks he is a robber, and they explain the killing.
Reluctantly, they allow him to join their troupe to replace the deceased member.

On their journey to the next town, they are forced to travel to a new district after a collapsed bridge stops them from taking their normal route and to mend the cart that carries their goods, although they have no money.
The troupe reaches a strange town, with its castle under reconstruction, and finds a woman being sentenced to death for killing a boy, upon the testimony of a monk (an actor).
The troupe performs a scriptural passion play, but, as told by the group's leader (an actor), so few attend they are unable to bury the dead troupe member and fix their cart.
The leader makes the decision to perform a new play based on the events surrounding the child's murder.
He and the priest visit the mute, condemned woman in the dungeons, coming away with the strong belief she is innocent.
The woman is portrayed as a seductress which infuriates the crowd and the parents of the dead boy, since he was virtuous and too physically strong to be overtaken by the woman.
The royal-house lord (an actor) watches from the castle and sends the sheriff to clear the square by force.
Members of the crowd, on leaving the square, tell the troupe about more details of the death or disappearance of boys.
The troupe is told to leave town by first light, but the priest's convictions urge him to determine first-hand what happened to the boy.
So in the night, the body is uncovered, and it is found to have been subjected to sodomy before death and also had been exposed to the plague.
The King's Justice and his squire comes upon the priest and they share some of their suspicions.
The priest is then forced to leave town, but before long returns in disguise as a monk.
The troupe remains on their journey to the city but the leader relinquishes his role as troupe leader and returns.
The priest is aware of the transitions in death from limber to rigor and returns.
He visits the monk who testified at trial to say all that he is aware of.
The monk reveals he had nothing to do with the death, intimating he is protecting someone else.
The priest leaves and is found by the leader.

The two of them then learn from the King's Justice that the monk has been found dead, and with it, any chance of evidence concerning the lord's proclivities, and also that the lord is planning a revolt to seize the English throne.
The sheriff reveals that it seems that wherever the lord goes, boys disappear.
The priest then obtains more evidence to prove that the woman is not the real killer (the body was found with rigor mortis, which meant the killing was more recent).
The execution is set but before it can be carried out, the troupe has returned and seized the scaffold as a stage for their new play based on the most recent information.

The crowd is incensed toward the lord and the guards are called out again to clear the town square, forcing the actors to the church and unknown to them, the lord is there performing an act of penitence.
The priest presents the evidence to the lord, who admits everything with an air of invulnerability, knowing that he is untouchable under the feudal system.
When the lord asks the priest about his sins, the priest confesses that he murdered the husband of the woman he was caught with, after he attacked the priest.
When leaving, the lord learns from the priest that he has been exposed to the plague.
The lord then stabs the priest, who stumbles outside the church.
The lord walks back to his castle through the throng of townsfolk, unaware of the revelations of the new play.
He reaches the gate to find that the portcullis is down and he is surrounded by the crowd, who lynch him and set fire to the castle.
The new authorities in the town hope the reason for the deaths will be forgotten.

The King's Justice promises that the priest's work will be told to the king, but a woman of the troupe replies that the priest didn't act for the king's sake, but for the wrongly accused, and his own redemption.
The leader announces that the priest will live on in their new play, which will be presented when they reach the city.
The troupe then departs while the castle is burned to the ground.
In 1993, the student (an actor), a US student at the university, wants the professor (an actor) as his thesis supervisor.
He idolises the professor and has learned all about him.
He takes accommodation in the city at the house of the landlady (an actress), an old friend of the professor.
Also in the house is her daughter, a young woman (an actress), who is her full-time caregiver – which she resents bitterly – and a musician by occupation.
In a public lecture, the professor quotes a philosopher's treatise to deny the possibility of absolute truth.
Hoping to impress his idol, the student disputes this, asserting his faith in the absolute truth of mathematics: "I believe in the number pi".
The professor humiliates him, ridiculing his arguments and making him look foolish in front of the audience.
Disillusioned, the student decides to abandon his studies and goes to his office to collect his belongings.
There, he encounters his office-mate, a bitter mathematician (an actor), who also failed to become a student of the professor's.
The student then returns to his residence, where he finds the professor arriving to visit the landlady.
The two men enter the house together and find the student's landlady murdered.
The professor tells the police that he had received a note with his friend's address marked as "the first of a series".
As the professor is an authority on logical series, he argues that a serial killer is using murder as a way to challenge his intelligence.
According to the professor, "The only perfect crime that exists is not the one that remains unsolved, but the one which is solved with the wrong culprit."
The student and the professor discuss how easily the murder of the old lady might have been overlooked, particularly as she already suffered from terminal cancer.

The student suggests that the murderer is committing "imperceptible murders", meaning that the killer is choosing victims who are already dying therefore meaning that the police would be less likely to suspect foul play.
The student goes to the hospital where his girlfriend (an actress) works.
There he meets a religious fanatic (an actor), who has a daughter in dire need of a lung transplant.
He also runs into the professor, who is visiting a friend (an actor), a former student who went mad and suffers from a debilitating cancer, with bone involvement.
Soon after, the patient who shares the room with the professor's friend dies of an apparent lethal injection and the authorities receive a second symbol: two interlocking arcs.
The student and the girlfriend's relationship becomes strained as he becomes more obsessed with the professor and the murders and discovers that the girlfriend had once been the professor's lover.

At a Guy Fawkes Night concert, the student sees the office-mate acting suspiciously and the police give chase, only to discover that the office-mate had merely intended to hang an insulting banner from the school roof.
While they are distracted a member of the orchestra collapses and dies from respiratory failure.
A drawing of a triangle is found on his music stand.
Afterwards, the professor tells the student a story about a nineteenth century man who had written a diary listing ways to kill his wife.
When the wife discovered the diary, she killed her husband but was acquitted by a jury on grounds of self-defence.
Decades later, the diary was discovered to have been forged by the woman's lover.
The professor uses this story to explain that the perfect crime is not one which is never solved, but one which is solved incorrectly.
All of the city's mathematics community is excited as a local researcher claims to have solved a famous theorem.
The mathematicians, including the professor and the student, board a bus to travel to the conference, but the student jumps out after seeing the girlfriend passing on the street.
The two reconcile and agree to take a long holiday away from the city, mathematics, and the professor.

After making love with the girlfriend, the student realises that the sequence the killer has sent them all consist of ancient mathematical symbols and that the fourth one will be a tetractys, consisting of ten points.
The police, thinking that the killer is obsessed with the professor, believe that he means to target the bus which the professor and the other mathematicians are travelling in.
However, the killer, as the student realises, is actually the man he had met at the hospital.
The man is a bus driver for a school for developmentally challenged children.
Seeing the students as unfit to live and wanting to provide organ donors to save his own daughter's life, he blows up the bus, killing the children and himself.

Afterwards, the police theorise that he had planned to escape the blast alive and had committed the other murders to present the deaths of the schoolchildren as the work of a serial murderer, thus shifting any blame from himself.
Afterwards, the girlfriend and the student prepare to leave the city.
However, the student realises that the professor has been lying to him the entire time.
As the girlfriend leaves in disgust, the student travels to meet the professor.
